questions.question: If you replace a basis vector by b_k ← b_k - r*b_j with integer r, what stays invariant?
options: The lattice generated by the basis
The Euclidean norms of all basis vectors
The Gram–Schmidt coefficients μ
The orthogonalized vectors b*
questions.explanation: Subtracting an integer multiple of another basis vector is a unimodular operation: it changes the basis but not the lattice.

questions.question: In LLL, what information from Gram–Schmidt is used to decide size reductions and swaps?
options: Projection coefficients μ_{k,j} and the squared lengths ||b*_k||^2
Only the determinant of the basis matrix
Only the Euclidean lengths ||b_k|| of the original vectors
Only the angles between the original vectors
questions.explanation: LLL uses Gram–Schmidt projection coefficients μ to size-reduce, and orthogonal lengths ||b*||^2 in the Lovász condition for swaps.

questions.question: Which inequality is the goal of LLL size reduction for all k > j?
options: det(B) = 1
questions.explanation: Size reduction enforces small projection coefficients: after reductions, all | μ_{k,j} | should be at most 1/2.

questions.question: When does LLL swap b_{k-1} and b_k?
options: When the Lovász condition fails at index k
Whenever ||b_k|| < ||b_{k-1}||
Whenever det(B) is negative
Whenever | μ_{k,k-1} | ≤ 1/2
questions.explanation: LLL swaps adjacent vectors specifically when the Lovász inequality is violated; the swap fixes an overly skew local configuration.

questions.question: What is the typical effect of increasing δ from 3/4 toward 1 (e.g., 0.99)?
options: Stronger reduction (often shorter vectors), but more work/swaps
Weaker reduction (often longer vectors), but more work/swaps
No effect on output or runtime
LLL becomes an exact shortest-vector algorithm
questions.explanation: Larger δ tightens the Lovász condition, typically forcing more swaps and yielding a more reduced (shorter/less skew) basis.

questions.question: Why can floating-point Gram–Schmidt cause problems in an educational LLL implementation on large integers?
options: Rounding noise can flip size-reduction and swap decisions, changing the output
Floating point makes the determinant invariant fail for integer matrices
Floating point forces the basis entries to become non-integers permanently
Floating point makes δ invalid (must be rational)
questions.explanation: LLL decisions depend on comparisons involving μ and ||b*||^2; floating-point error can change those comparisons and lead to different (or incorrect) behavior.

questions.question: Attack intuition: why is publishing a long, skew basis not a reliable way to hide that the lattice contains short vectors?
options: Unimodular basis changes preserve the lattice, and reduction can often reveal much shorter vectors
Because the determinant always equals the shortest vector length
Because any lattice basis must contain the shortest vector as one of its columns
Because size reduction alone always solves exact SVP
questions.explanation: A basis is just a coordinate system; the lattice itself is unchanged by unimodular transformations. Reduction algorithms can often recover short vectors even from very skew bases.

questions.question: Which statement is true about what LLL guarantees?
options: It runs in polynomial time and outputs an LLL-reduced basis, but does not guarantee the shortest vector
It always outputs the exact shortest non-zero lattice vector in any dimension
It finds the closest lattice vector to any target (exact CVP) in polynomial time
It works only in 2D and fails in higher dimensions
questions.explanation: LLL is a polynomial-time basis reduction algorithm with provable quality guarantees, but it is not an exact SVP/CVP solver in general.
